title: Goyal Leads 200-Member Business Delegation to Japan, Pitches India as $30 Trillion Partner
excerpt: Commerce Minister targets 10 trillion yen in Japanese investment over the next decade across AI, semiconductors, and clean energy as bilateral trade hits $27.5 billion.
body:
• Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal led a 200-member Indian business delegation to Japan at the UP-Japan Investment Meet 2026, pitching India’s $30 trillion growth vision.
  • Bilateral trade between India and Japan stood at $27.5 billion in FY 2025-26, with both sides targeting 10 trillion yen in Japanese investment over the next decade.
  • Key sectors identified for collaboration include artificial intelligence, semiconductors, critical minerals, batteries, energy, and next-generation mobility.
  • Japan is India’s fifth-largest source of FDI, with more than 1,400 Japanese companies already operating in the country across 11 industrial townships in eight states.

India Makes Its Case in Tokyo

Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal led a delegation of more than 200 Indian industrialists, chief executives, and business leaders to Japan for the UP-Japan Investment Meet 2026, held from August 18 to 23. The visit marked one of India’s largest coordinated business missions to Japan in recent years, with the delegation meeting counterparts from companies including Hitachi, Daikin, Panasonic, Omron, and HORIBA, according to CNBC TV18.

https://x.com/TimesNow/status/2091782319749353660

“Our bilateral trade stands at around $27.5 billion in FY 2025-26, still a fraction of our potential,” Goyal told the Japanese delegation, according to The Hindu BusinessLine. He outlined a target of 10 trillion yen in Japanese investment in India over the coming decade, spanning technologies “that will shape our future.”

“Warmth and trust are at the heart of our relationship, and it is matched by strategic ambition with a clear number: 10 trillion yen of Japanese investment in India over the next decade.”

— Piyush Goyal, Commerce and Industry Minister

Sectors on the Table

Goyal identified artificial intelligence, semiconductors, critical minerals, batteries, energy, and next-generation mobility as the primary areas for deepened collaboration. The investment pitch comes as global supply chains continue to realign away from China, positioning India as a strategic manufacturing alternative for Japanese mid-sized companies looking to diversify.

The minister pointed to existing anchors of the relationship: the Mumbai-Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail project, Japanese-assisted metro systems in Delhi, Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, and Chennai, and 11 Japanese industrial townships spread across eight Indian states. Japan is currently India’s fifth-largest source of foreign direct investment, with more than 1,400 Japanese companies operating in the country, including Suzuki, Toyota, Honda, Sony, Hitachi, and Mitsubishi.

Uttar Pradesh as the Investment Magnet

Goyal made a specific pitch for Uttar Pradesh, India’s most populous state and its third-largest economy. He cited the state’s ambition to become a $1 trillion economy, its more than nine million micro, small, and medium enterprises, and its position as the country’s fifth-largest state exporter.

“UP offers a unique platform for Japan’s technological strength and experienced mature demographic to meet India’s young workforce and growing market,” Goyal said, adding that the state would be “at the centre point of our journey towards a developed India” under Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath’s leadership.

The Japanese delegation was led by Yamanashi Prefecture Governor Kotaro Nagasaki.

Broader Strategic Context

The visit builds on a series of India-Japan economic engagements in 2026. In May, Goyal held talks with a Japanese delegation led by Takayuki Kobayashi, Chairperson of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party’s Policy Research Council, to strengthen MSME partnerships and deepen collaboration in automobiles, infrastructure, pharmaceuticals, and advanced manufacturing. Those discussions also explored future pathways under the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA).

India and Japan adopted a Joint Vision for the Next Decade during Prime Minister Modi’s 2025 Tokyo visit, encouraging SME cooperation between the two nations. The trade relationship, however, remains imbalanced — India has historically pushed for greater gains from the bilateral CEPA, which has so far benefitted Japan more than India, according to The Hindu BusinessLine.

What’s Next

With U.S. reciprocal tariffs disrupting trade patterns for both India and Japan, the two countries are exploring ways to offset the impact through deeper bilateral ties. The delegation visit signals India’s intent to position itself as Japan’s preferred manufacturing and investment partner in Asia, competing directly with Vietnam, Indonesia, and other Southeast Asian alternatives for Japanese capital.
